title: Asymptotic Gotsman–Linial conjecture
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
formal: Does there exist a universal constant \(C>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), every \(1\le d\le n\), and every Boolean function \(f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\{-1,1\}\) represented as the sign of a real polynomial of degree at most \(d\), \[I(f)\le C d\sqrt n?\] Here \(I(f)\) is total influence, the expected number of input coordinates whose flip changes the output at a uniformly random input. The precise polynomial and tie conventions are defined below. The same constant must work for growing degrees as well as fixed degrees.
definitions:
Let \(\mathcal F_{n,d}\) denote the polynomial threshold functions specified below, and let \(M(n,d)=\max_{f\in\mathcal F_{n,d}}I(f)\). 

Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A real multilinear polynomial of degree at most \(d\) has the form
\[p(x)=\sum_{\substack{S\subseteq[n]\\|S|\le d}}a_S\prod_{i\in S}x_i,\qquad a_S\in\mathbb R,\]
with empty product \(1\). All coefficients are unrestricted reals; there is no bound on their magnitude, bit length, the number of nonzero monomials, or the minimum nonzero value of \(|p|\) on the cube. Require \(p(x)\ne0\) at every \(x\in\{-1,1\}^n\). Its threshold function is \(f(x)=+1\) when \(p(x)>0\), and \(f(x)=-1\) when \(p(x)<0\). The class \(\mathcal F_{n,d}\) contains every function with at least one such representation, not just those whose least possible threshold degree is exactly \(d\). Starting with arbitrary real polynomials gives the same class: reducing powers using \(x_i^2=1\) preserves the cube values and does not increase degree. Excluding zeros fixes the tie convention; any representation using one fixed value of sign at zero can be perturbed by a sufficiently small constant to remove its cube zeros without changing the function.

Choose \(x\) uniformly from all \(2^n\) cube points, with independent equally likely coordinates. For \(i\in[n]\), let \(x^{\oplus i}\) have coordinate \(-x_i\) at \(i\) and agree with \(x\) elsewhere. Define
\[\operatorname{Inf}_i(f)=2^{-n}|\{x:f(x)\ne f(x^{\oplus i})\}|,\quad s_f(x)=|\{i\in[n]:f(x)\ne f(x^{\oplus i})\}|,\]
\[I(f)=\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{Inf}_i(f)=2^{-n}\sum_{x\in\{-1,1\}^n}s_f(x).\]
Thus total influence is average sensitivity, not maximum pointwise sensitivity and not influence divided by \(n\). There is no biased input distribution or additional probability over polynomials. The maximization is over Boolean functions; different coefficient choices representing the same function have the same influence. It is a maximum rather than merely a supremum because only finitely many Boolean functions exist on a fixed cube, and \(\mathcal F_{n,d}\) is nonempty. Constants belong to the class with influence zero, while a dictator \(f(x)=x_1\) has influence one; hence \(1\le M(n,d)\le n\) on the stated domain.

The constants in the answer must be absolute: they cannot depend on degree, dimension, a representation, or an asymptotic path through the parameter pairs. The estimates must hold throughout the domain, including small dimensions and growing degrees; finite exceptional cases must be covered by the proved constants. This is a mathematical extremal-growth problem, with no evaluation-time requirement or finite encoding assumption for real coefficients. The omitted degree-zero case has value zero, and degrees larger than \(n\) give no additional Boolean functions, so the displayed domain covers all nontrivial regimes.
answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed assertion or of its logical negation, with exactly the stated model, quantifier order and parameter dependence. A bound for a restricted subclass or one particular algorithm is insufficient to refute a universal existence assertion. Determining the entire optimal rate or a numerical approximation to it is not required.

progress.text: Kane proves the \(\sqrt n\) exponent up to logarithmic factors depending on degree; the preprint, CCC presentation and journal version have different dates.
Kim–Maldonado–Wellens establish influence estimates for structured quadratic coefficient graphs.
Chapman disproves the original exact extremizer conjecture while preserving the asymptotic open question.
Chapman’s MIT thesis again distinguishes the exact, asymptotic and weaker polylogarithmic formulations.
Kothari and coauthors’ revised rational-degree paper restates the conjecture and proposes a weaker nondeterministic-degree analogue in §5.2.
Chang and coauthors’ second revision proves polylogarithmic Boolean surface area for fixed-degree PTFs, a different moment from total influence.

status_note: Checked through 16 September 2026. The exact symmetric-extremizer conjecture is false, but no universal joint constant-factor determination of M(n,d) was found in the bounded primary-source review. The surviving O(d sqrt(n)) influence bound is explicitly still a conjecture in the checked April2026 revisions. The Boolean surface-area theorem bounds a different sensitivity moment with degree-dependent logarithmic factors, and the rational-degree theorem concerns a different degree comparison. New proofs were not independently certified.

context_blocks.text: The selected target is the asymptotic Gotsman–Linial conjecture \(I(f)=O(d\sqrt n)\), uniformly in dimension and degree. It is distinct from the stronger, disproved assertion that one particular symmetric function is an exact maximizer.

A polynomial threshold function evaluates a real polynomial and keeps its sign. Linear threshold functions include majority and weighted voting rules; degree two also permits pairwise interactions. Threshold degree measures the degree needed to represent the sign pattern, rather than the degree needed to equal the Boolean function numerically on every input.

Total influence is the expected number of sensitive coordinates at a uniformly random input. If \(D(f)\) is the number of undirected cube edges joining opposite outputs, then \(I(f)=2^{1-n}D(f)\). By contrast, the probability that flipping one uniformly chosen coordinate changes the output is \(I(f)/n\). The normalization in the target is the former, which ranges from zero to \(n\).

For odd \(n\), majority has \[I(\operatorname{MAJ}_n)=n\,2^{1-n}\binom{n-1}{(n-1)/2}\sim\sqrt{2n/\pi}.\] Thus influence already grows with dimension at degree one. At the opposite endpoint, parity \(f(x)=\prod_{i=1}^n x_i\) has degree \(n\) and influence \(n\), so \(M(n,n)=n\).

The classical symmetric examples change sign across consecutive central Hamming layers. Their total influence has order \(\min\{n,d\sqrt n\}\), with constants uniform in the two parameters. This supplies the standard lower scale, including saturation at large degree. Gotsman and Linial conjectured that such an example actually maximizes influence exactly; the remaining asymptotic question permits different maximizers.

Chapman’s counterexamples refute that exact assertion for \(d=2\) in every odd dimension \(n\ge5\), and for \(n\ge7\) with \(3\le d\le n-3\). They do not rule out a universal \(O(d\sqrt n)\) upper bound. Combined with the elementary upper bound \(I(f)\le n\) and the standard lower scale, that surviving conjecture would give \(M(n,d)=\Theta(\min\{n,d\sqrt n\})\).

The common constants are part of the mathematical target. Bounds \(M(n,d)\le C_d\sqrt n\) with an unspecified degree-dependent constant \(C_d\) do not determine the joint dependence on \(n,d\). Nor does an estimate only as \(n\to\infty\) with \(d\) fixed cover sequences of increasing degree. The requested bound must also cover the transition to influence of order \(n\).

Kane’s Theorem 2 gives \(I(f)\le\sqrt n\,(\log n)^{O(d\log d)}2^{O(d^2\log d)}\) for \(d\ge2\). For every fixed degree this has the correct power of \(n\), up to logarithmic factors. Those factors still grow with dimension, and the bound’s dependence on degree is much larger than linear, so it does not give matching universal factors in the requested joint regime.

For quadratic threshold functions, Kim, Maldonado and Wellens study the graph whose edges mark nonzero coefficients of pairwise monomials. Their Theorems 1.2 and 1.3 give bounds in terms of the graph’s fractional chromatic number and its number of edges. These are structural estimates for a prescribed representation, not a matching bound for all dense quadratic representations.

The April 27, 2026 revision by Chang, Slote, Volberg and Zhang proves a fixed-degree polylogarithmic bound on Boolean surface area, defined by \(\operatorname{BSA}(f)=\mathbb E_x\sqrt{s_f(x)}\). Its Theorem 1.1 has constants depending on degree. The paper explicitly distinguishes this fractional sensitivity moment from total influence \(\mathbb E_x s_f(x)\).
A proof or refutation of this universal upper bound answers the card. Determining the full extremal function after a refutation is not required.

Kothari, Kovacs-Deak, Wang and Yang’s April 2026 revision establishes a polynomial relationship between rational degree and ordinary degree. Its §5.2 restates the asymptotic influence conjecture and proposes a weaker nondeterministic-degree analogue. Neither that main degree theorem nor the proposed weaker conjecture determines the maximum influence of arbitrary polynomial threshold functions.

A matching joint bound would quantify how strongly a low-degree sign representation constrains the edge boundary of a Boolean function. This connects algebraic representation to sensitivity, noise behavior and learning-theoretic complexity. A solution may establish the surviving conjectured scale or a different scale, but disproving one particular candidate without determining the extremal growth does not complete the task.
